case_study_insert.main_stem: Pinnacle Dental Care (PDC) is a private limited company in the dental healthcare sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Dr Elena Shaw, the business runs six high-street practices and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. PDC plans to invest $720,000 in three new dental surgery suites with digital imaging, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $35 a unit and a selling price of $95 for routine treatment, and currently provides 12,000 units a year. PDC faces two problems: 15 of its clinical staff have not completed on-the-job training on the imaging system, and patient complaints about an 11-day appointment waiting time are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Patient Survey and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The practices completed 1,850 appointments in September at an 88% patient satisfaction score, while the rework rate was 2.4%, down from 3.1% a year earlier. Formal complaint letters rose from 26 to 42 per month, and average waiting time for a routine appointment is 11 days. A survey of 500 registered patients found that 71% would pay $15 more for same-day appointments and 64% choose a dentist on the basis of modern equipment. 15 of the 60 clinical staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new digital imaging system; an external certification course costs $480 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Pinnacle Dental Care for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans such as PDC's $450,000 expansion loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $13.50 to $14.30 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for clinical and reception staff. (3) Private dental insurance reimbursement rates have been cut by 4.5%, and the cost of composite and imaging consumables has risen 9.2% year-on-year, while consumer spending on private dental care grew 2.8%.

questions.question_text: PDC plans to fund part of its $720,000 surgery expansion with a $450,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for PDC of using $270,000 retained profit instead of that loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs PDC nothing in interest or capital repayments, protecting cash flow while it already meets fixed costs of $360,000 a year. Every dollar not paid to the bank can instead absorb the 9.2% rise in imaging and composite consumables or fund the 15 clinical staff still needing training on the digital imaging system, rather than being lost as finance charges on the $720,000 three-suite expansion.

Point 2: Using $270,000 retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk, so the new surgery suites cannot be at risk if patient demand for the 12,000 units of routine treatment falls short of forecast. It also preserves the ownership and control built up since Dr Elena Shaw founded the practices in 2011, because no lender can impose conditions on how the new imaging service is run. A larger bank loan would commit PDC to fixed repayments regardless of patient numbers, which is risky when an 11-day appointment waiting time already shows capacity under strain.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to PDC's expansion, costs and staffing.

questions.question_text: PDC wants to fill the appointment gaps left by its 11-day waiting time. Consider local newspaper and radio advertising, a patient referral incentive, or a targeted social media campaign. Which should PDC choose to attract new patients? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local newspaper and radio advertising: These channels would reach older, locally based patients across the six high-street practice catchments and build trust quickly for a healthcare service. However, airtime and print costs are high, much of the audience is outside PDC's neighbourhoods, and a general message does not communicate the specific advantage of the new digital imaging suites, so spend would be wasted for a 60-employee firm already funding a $720,000 expansion.

Patient referral incentive: Offering existing satisfied patients a credit to recommend friends exploits the 88% satisfaction score and the fact that 71% of 500 surveyed patients already value same-day appointments. Referrals are cheap and trusted, but growth is slow and depends on patients actively recommending; it cannot rapidly fill the 11-day waiting-time gap or create demand for three new suites.

Targeted social media campaign: Online ads can be geo-fenced around the six practices and aimed at the 64% of surveyed patients who choose a dentist on modern equipment, showing the new digital imaging directly. Results are measurable, cost per enquiry is low, and same-day availability can be promoted instantly; the drawback is weaker reach among older patients who still rely on local press.

Recommendation: PDC should choose the targeted social media campaign, supported by a small referral incentive. It reaches the exact segment identified in the survey, promotes the new imaging at low cost, and can be scaled nationally as the new suites open. Newspaper and radio advertising is rejected as expensive and untargeted; referral alone is rejected as too slow to close an 11-day waiting-time problem.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal reference to PDC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of PDC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a justified recommendation that explains why newspaper/radio and referral alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: PDC's flat structure and democratic leadership are said to improve motivation. Explain two benefits for PDC of this approach in reducing its 11-day appointment waiting time and 42 monthly complaints.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 60 employees a real voice in how the three new surgery suites and imaging routines are organised, which supports their social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Reception and clinical staff who help redesign appointment scheduling are more likely to commit to the changes, so the 11-day waiting time can be tackled by staff who understand the bottlenecks rather than by instructions imposed from above.

Point 2: A flat structure shortens the chain of command, so suggestions from the 15 staff not yet trained on digital imaging reach Dr Elena Shaw quickly and can be acted on before complaints grow beyond the current 42 a month. Involvement also builds ownership of the 2.4% rework rate, encouraging staff to propose small improvements that protect the 88% satisfaction score while PDC expands from six to nine practices. Flatter decision-making also lets Dr Elena Shaw act on the 88% satisfaction feedback quickly, protecting patient loyalty while the three new suites are opening.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to PDC's waiting time, complaints and satisfaction data.

questions.question_text: PDC must upskill 15 of its clinical staff on the new digital imaging system. Consider on-the-job training or an external certification course at $480 per employee. Which should PDC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the chairside is directly relevant to PDC's own imaging equipment, costs no course fees, and keeps all 15 staff seeing patients while they learn, which protects appointment capacity while the 11-day waiting time is already a problem. It also lets experienced colleagues model the 2.4% rework standard. The weakness is that trainers are working clinicians whose own throughput falls, bad habits can be copied, and there is no externally recognised certificate for the three new surgery suites.

External certification course: At $480 per employee, the full 15-person course costs $7,200 (15 × $480) — small against the $720,000 expansion. It gives structured, up-to-date skills and a certificate that supports quality assurance claims to patients, and it removes staff from the busy practices so training is not squeezed. However, it takes 15 clinicians off the rota temporarily, worsening the 11-day wait, and the generic content may not match PDC's exact imaging settings without follow-up coaching.

The richer clinical record also helps when applying for the referral partnerships that could fill the new suites, but the insert gives no evidence that formal certification reduces the 2.4% rework rate, so this benefit should not be overstated.

Decision: PDC should choose on-the-job training first, with short external certification top-ups later for senior operators. On-the-job training protects patient capacity when waiting time is already 11 days, is free, and is machine-specific; full external training is rejected because losing 15 staff from six practices would deepen the 42-complaint problem and the $7,200 fee duplicates skills that can be learned on site.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to PDC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of PDC's waiting time and costs.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to digital imaging.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how PDC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($95 − $35) = $360,000 ÷ $60 = 6,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 6,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $95 − $35 = $60. Answer: contribution per unit is $60.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways PDC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 6,000-unit break-even output with 12,000 units actually provided shows a margin of safety of 6,000 units, confirming the six practices are profitable and giving confidence to open three more suites.
2. Contribution of $60 a unit lets managers model a discount on the $95 routine fee; for example, a $5 cut leaves $55 contribution, still above the $35 variable cost, and shows the extra volume needed to cover $360,000 fixed costs.
3. With fixed costs of $360,000 and contribution of $60, managers can set the treatment-volume target needed to service the $450,000 loan before committing to the $720,000 expansion.
4. Average total cost ($360,000 ÷ 12,000 + $35 = $65) can be benchmarked each quarter to detect waste from the 2.4% rework rate and to judge whether the 9.2% consumables inflation is being controlled.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 6,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $60 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs 12,000-unit output; discount modelling on the $95 fee; loan-repayment volume target for the $450,000 loan; and average total cost of $65 to monitor rework and consumables inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate PDC's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has PDC's performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 60.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 63.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: 2024: 1,440 ÷ 2,400 × 100 = 60.0%; 360 ÷ 2,400 × 100 = 15.0%; 360 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 18.0%. 2025: 1,890 ÷ 3,000 × 100 = 63.0%; 540 ÷ 3,000 × 100 = 18.0%; 540 ÷ 2,400 × 100 = 22.5%. Revenue rose to $3,000,000 while cost of sales increased only to $1,110,000, so the first margin widened; operating profit grew to $540,000 as the second margin and the return on the $2,400,000 capital base both strengthened. Interest payable fell from $40,000 to $35,000, so more operating profit is retained.

Evaluation: Every measure moved favourably. The first margin rising from 60.0% to 63.0% shows better control of clinical consumables despite the 9.2% input-cost rise in the bulletin. The 15.0% to 18.0% rise in operating profitability shows fixed costs of $360,000 are being spread over a larger revenue base from 12,000 treatment units. The return on capital employed improving from 18.0% to 22.5% is the strongest signal, because it shows the existing asset base is generating more profit, which supports the $720,000 investment. A caution is that receivables and cash are not shown here, so a strong income statement does not prove short-term solvency, and the $450,000 loan still needs servicing.

Conclusion: PDC's performance has clearly improved. All three measures rose together, and the 22.5% return on capital employed confirms that growth is creating value rather than merely increasing revenue.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate percentage calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates all three measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PDC of charging the $15 premium for same-day appointments identified in its patient survey.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 500 patients found that 71% would pay $15 more for same-day appointments, so the premium could raise the average selling price above the current $95 routine fee and lift contribution per unit from $60 toward $75 on those bookings. That extra contribution would help cover the fixed costs of $360,000 a year and speed repayment of the $450,000 loan, while directly reducing the 11-day appointment waiting time by spreading demand.

Disadvantage: charging more may put off the 29% of surveyed patients who would not pay the premium, potentially leaving capacity idle in the three new surgery suites and slowing growth from the current 12,000 units. It may also raise expectations of faster service: if the 42 monthly complaints are not resolved, paying patients could be less tolerant, damaging the 88% satisfaction score that PDC relies on to win referrals. Managers should therefore trial the premium on a limited number of same-day slots before applying it across all six practices.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to PDC's survey data, contribution and service problems.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.2% rise in clinical consumables costs will affect PDC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If PDC's $450,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $360,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. Higher rates may also cool demand for private dental care and raise the cost of future borrowing for the $720,000 expansion, but PDC could cap this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $14.30 an hour): With a workforce of 60, including reception and support staff, this feeds into the wage bill and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented. The honest test is productivity: 12,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 200 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if output per worker holds or grows, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $60 contribution per unit shrinks.

Clinical consumables inflation (9.2%): The $35 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound can be calculated: if the whole variable cost rose 9.2% it would add 0.092 × $35 = $3.22 per unit; at 12,000 units that is $38,640 a year. Even a smaller rise cuts the $60 contribution on every routine treatment, and the 4.5% reimbursement cut limits PDC's ability to pass costs on, though the $15 same-day premium offers partial recovery.

Conclusion: The 9.2% rise in consumables has the greatest impact. It compounds across all 12,000 units, directly erodes the $60 contribution that justifies the $720,000 investment, and is reinforced by the reimbursement cut; the interest rise is only $3,375 a year and the wage effect, while real, cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity and the premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to PDC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on PDC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that consumables inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
